tagline.text: The cathedral of Our Lady of the Pillar, seat of the Diocese of Imus, which covers all of Cavite

location.label: Location
location.text: Central Imus, Cavite, close to the city plaza

children.text: Imus Cathedral is the seat of the Diocese of Imus, which covers the whole province of Cavite, and a diocesan shrine to Our Lady of the Pillar. Construction of this Baroque church began in the early 19th century, a historical marker was placed in 2006 by the national historical commission, and it is also known for its long Holy Week procession.

The official name of Imus Cathedral is the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Our Lady of the Pillar. It stands in the city of Imus, Cavite, and is the cathedral of the Diocese of Imus, which covers the entire province. It lies about
20km

south of central Manila, which makes it an easy day trip. The location is in the heart of the city, near the city plaza, and markets and shops line the surrounding streets, so you can see everyday local life as well.

The history goes back to the Spanish colonial era. In 1616 Augustinian Recollect friars came to Imus and founded a convent, and the parish is said to have started as a small chapel dependent on Cavite Viejo (today's Kawit). Imus became an independent town and parish on October 3, 1795, and its first church stood in the village of Bayan Luma. Later, Fr. Nicolas Becerra moved the town center in 1823 to the area of Balangon, where the church stands today, and began building the new church; construction was completed in 1853. For a long time the land around Imus belonged to the Augustinian Recollects. The order began buying land in 1666, and by around 1812 the Hacienda de San Juan de Imus had taken shape, said to have covered Imus, Dasmariñas and part of Kawit. On March 31, 1894 the hacienda was sold to a company in Madrid for 4,000,000 pesetas, and it later passed through a British company to the Philippine government under American rule. In 1897 the church became a diocesan parish, run by diocesan priests rather than the religious order.
The church is a Baroque building of brick and tuff stone. It is known to be about
long and
wide, with an estimated height of about

, and its façade is said to be modeled on the fifth Manila Cathedral. On November 13, 2006 the National Historical Institute (now the NHCP) placed a marker declaring it a structure of historical significance, and on December 3, 2012 the image of Our Lady of the Pillar received its canonical coronation, presided over by Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle. Among the bishops who served at this cathedral is Luis Antonio Tagle, who later became Archbishop of Manila and a cardinal. The first bishop of the diocese was Artemio Casas, and Bishop Reynaldo Evangelista, installed on June 5, 2013, is the fifth bishop.
Imus Cathedral is an active cathedral dedicated to Our Lady of the Pillar. Look up “Our Lady of the Pillar – City of Imus Proper” in the
Diocese of Imus parish directory
for parish information. To visit Emilio Aguinaldo Shrine, associated with the declaration of independence, continue to neighboring Kawit.
This 19th-century Baroque church is built of brick and tuff stone. Its façade is said to be modeled on Manila Cathedral, and the long nave, about
in length, catches the eye in the middle of the city.

blocks.title: Image of Our Lady of the Pillar

children.text: This is the main Marian image venerated in the church, and it received its canonical coronation on December 3, 2012. The feast of Our Lady is on
October 12
, and the faithful gather in numbers around that time.

blocks.title: Seat of the Diocese of Cavite

children.text: This is the central church of the Diocese of Imus, which covers the whole province of Cavite. The diocese was created in 1961 by an apostolic constitution of Pope John XXIII, and its formal erection as the Diocese of Imus is said to have been in April 1962.

The marker placed by the National Historical Institute on November 13, 2006 officially recognizes the historical value of the building. It invites you to reflect on the history of the Imus parish laid down by the Augustinian Recollects.

blocks.title: The longest Holy Week procession in Cavite

children.text: During Holy Week the procession is famous for at least 70 floats in a long line and is described as the longest Holy Week procession in Cavite. If you want to see the atmosphere of the week before Easter, this is the most striking time to visit.

blocks.title: City plaza and a walk through Imus

children.text: The church stands close to the city plaza, the site of the old Balangon. The plaza has a national historical marker installed in 1954, so you can walk through the history of central Imus together with the church.

blocks.title: Parishes and chapels of the diocese

children.text: The cathedral parish oversees several chapels, such as those in Bayan Luma, Toclong and Tanzang Luma, and nearby are parishes of the Vicariate of Our Lady of the Pillar such as Immaculate Heart of Mary, Our Lady of Fatima and Holy Family. You can feel how the central church is the heart of the local faith community.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From the cathedral to the historical sites downtown

children.text: Leave Manila. It is best to head for Imus before traffic builds up, as Aguinaldo Highway can be congested during rush hours.
Arrive at Imus Cathedral and first look around the exterior and façade. Find the historical marker and read the inscription.
If no service is in progress, quietly walk through the nave. Look at the image of Our Lady of the Pillar, the altar and the ceiling, and take photos politely, reading the mood around you.
Walk around the city plaza to see the site of the old Balangon and the historical marker installed in 1954. There is also a monument commemorating the 1896 Battle of Imus in the city.
Have lunch around the city market. Prices and hours at local eateries change often, so check on the spot.
See more of central Imus, or continue to Kawit for Aguinaldo Shrine, the site of the declaration of independence.
Interior viewing may be restricted during services and events, so check the cathedral's official social media announcements before you go.
The usual way is to take a bus or jeepney from southern Manila (the Pasay and Baclaran area) toward Cavite and continue to Imus. Routes and boarding points change often, so check locally.
Imus is about
20km
from central Manila, and depending on traffic the trip can take
1–2 hours
or more.
Once in the city, transfer to a tricycle or jeepney heading to the city plaza.
Aguinaldo Highway (General Emilio Aguinaldo Highway) runs through Imus from north to south. It is very congested during rush hours.
Taxis and ride-hailing apps are convenient, but fares depend heavily on traffic. Check how the fare is calculated before you board.
The area around the church has markets and shops and is busy even on weekday afternoons. Check parking on the spot.
Tricycles and jeepneys are the main way to get around Imus.
The cathedral and the city plaza are within walking distance of each other.

Imus has the same tropical climate as the rest of the Philippines, and the church can be visited both inside and out, so you can go at any time of year. To avoid midday heat and heavy rain, mornings in the dry season are the most comfortable.

If you want to see the church at its most atmospheric, Holy Week or the days around the feast of Our Lady of the Pillar are best. Crowds come for the processions and Masses at those times, so allow for the schedule and the congestion.

In November 2009 the city of Imus hosted the 5th Asian Youth Day, a sign that the city has also served as a stage for Church events. Checking the diocese's announcements before you visit helps you avoid missing special events.

Imus Cathedral is an easy day trip from Manila, so most visitors return the same day without staying overnight. There are places to stay in Imus itself, but the choice is limited, so if you want to spend a night, also look at accommodation in Tagaytay or Cavite City. Rates and availability vary a lot, so check before booking.

Food centers on the markets, shops and street stalls around the church. You can enjoy simple meals and street snacks found all over the Philippines cheaply, but there are not many famous restaurants known specifically in Imus, so asking local residents is the most reliable way to find a good place.

The city of Imus holds events every year around National Flag Day on May 28, the anniversary of the Battle of Imus on September 3, and the October 12 feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, and it is busier than usual then. Lodging can be hard to find during events, so book ahead and prepare for traffic congestion.
The church is still used for worship today. Modest clothing that covers shoulders and knees is recommended.
During Mass, avoid taking photos and talking loudly, and it is polite to remove your hat before entering.
The days around Holy Week and the October 12 feast of Our Lady of the Pillar are very crowded, so arrive early or visit outside those periods.
Walking between the city plaza and the church is an efficient route. The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat and water.
Mass times and opening hours can change. Check the church's official Facebook page or the diocese's announcements before you visit.
City roads are very congested, so allow plenty of travel time and keep valuables in front of your body.
The diocese runs its own broadcasting, such as a radio station (89.5 FM) that relays Masses at low power, so have a look if you are interested.
This is a place of worship, so avoid noise and revealing clothing, and check Mass and event schedules before you visit.
Interior viewing may be restricted during Mass times and events.
Traffic on the Aguinaldo Highway section is heavy during rush hours.
Watch for pickpockets in crowded areas around the market and church.
When taking photos, be careful not to put the faces of worshippers prominently in the frame.
Follow local notices for fees and hours near the church.
The
Emilio Aguinaldo Shrine
in Kawit, Cavite, is the site of the Philippine declaration of independence. Allow separate travel time to Kawit if visiting it and Imus Cathedral on the same day.

This entry introduces the whole city where the church stands. In Imus, nicknamed the Flag Capital since the Battle of Alapan in 1898, you can combine sightseeing with historical sites; there is a national heritage park in Alapan, and the Imus Historical Museum hosts reenactments of Revolution-era scenes.
A city that preserves the history of the Spanish-era port and fortress. It is about
40 minutes–1 hour
by car from Imus.
A cool highland resort. It takes about
1–2 hours
by car to the south of Imus, and it suits an itinerary that includes an overnight stay.
